data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"A decision procedure strictly polynomial in the number of coins n alone is achievable, running in O(n^3) time, and it correctly finds the smallest counterexample for non-canonical coin systems.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the smallest counterexample is not within the restricted polynomial-sized set of candidates evaluated by Pearson's algorithm, it will falsely conclude canonicity.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If bit complexity is considered and arithmetic operations cost O(log c_1), the running time becomes O(n^3 log c_1), violating the strictly polynomial-in-n claim.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the algorithm fails to correctly handle base cases where n < 3, it might produce incorrect results or errors.","eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Pearson's algorithm (2005) achieves O(n^3) time complexity by evaluating canonicity using only a polynomial number of candidate amounts. It checks optimal and greedy representations for amounts constructed from combinations of coins (specifically residues of multiples of c_i modulo c_j). It finds the minimal counterexample among these candidates without depending on the magnitude c_1.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
